gyros is just really thin cuts of meat stacked on top of each other on a massive skewer and then shaved away once the outside layers get nice and crispy. It's not high calorie by itself, honestly, for how filling it is. Gyros should not be chunky, ever. Chunky gyros is a sign of a very low-quality "cook". It's also usually undercooked (if you get undercooked chicken gyros, someone should pray for you). The main ingredients in the average pita-gyros with pork, is:

  • the pita- which, at least here in Greece is about 150 calories each (depends on brand honestly, like most things), let's say 200 if you really drench it in oil for some insane fucking reason instead of just very lightly glazing it (most places no longer use any oil while cooking the pita).

  • the meat- most of the calories come from this if you pick pork gyros, let's say around 350 cals at most (a lot of places use good quality meat nowadays, with a lot less fat than they used to, which means lower calories) because it doesn't really have that much inside of it. Like, way less than what's shown in that abomination of an image. Usually, it's about 100 grams. Again, nothing is added to the meat except salt, pepper, and maybe paprika. No oil is added anyway because the cooking process forbids it. It's cooked only in its own juices, nothing else. No oil, certainly no butter or anything.

  • various calorically insignificant veggies like tomato and onion and lettuce, as well as about a heaped teaspoon/a normal tablespoon of tzatziki (which is straight up nothing but real yogurt with garlic and tiny bits of cucumber. Some people put oil in it, but that's wrong and they are wrong and also heathens and it just sticks to the roof of your mouth if you do that). Tzatziki made the right way has less calories than mayo (even made the wrong way I think it's still less). A tablespoon can be 40-75 calories depending on yogurt used to make it.

  • some people choose to put fries in it (as in the image), but not this many, at all. Most places don't put more than 5-7 in anyway, because then it just tastes wrong and it's hard to wrap properly (what's in the pics is not, in fact, wrapped properly). I'd argue if someone really wants the potatoes, they just get them as a side.

If you wanna go even lower, get skewers (either pork or chicken; I've had beef, too, which wasn't great anyway). Both are decent options, there's not that huge a difference between them. Skewers are about 200 calories (at most, usually it's 170-180) for pork and like 130 for a big chicken one. Going by what is considered the average weight of a skewer, of course. Here it's about... 110-130 grams per skewer. Again, really low cal compared to everything else you can get to go (even just homemade plain pasta is worse, especially if you're also considering that at least this has some protein in it and is actually filling).

We don't really have big chain restaurants here, for the most part, which means we also don't have adverts or promos with food in them- we don't have Burger King or anything else, McD's is shit anyway, KFC and Starbucks both only exist here in Athens and are doing really badly because only tourists go there (we do have KFC "style" ripoff shops, but they're better quality and cheaper, so Greeks just go there instead if they want fried chicken). Starbucks especially is only supported by fatties. Souvlaki is really cheap (one pita-gyros is usually around 2.30 Euro, sometimes less) and it's not a bad option by comparison- obviously not to eat every day, but honestly? And they're all either jacked or underweight. The really underweight ones obviously eat nothing else all day. Even two of them is still below 1000 calories, even if you make it with pork, add oil to the pita, and add the fries. Again, it's quite filling, so it's not like you can eat this and then eat something else. Also not something you can eat if you've had a "heavy" lunch, anyway.

I know some former males, sure, but they all eat American-style. Massive pizzas with weird things on them and huge burgers and giant bowls of pasta and donuts and weird concoctions of cheese and bacon and constantly chugging full-sugar soda and all that shit. I eat some of those things occasionally (minus the soda, never got the hype honestly)- not in this quantity, not in this frequency, not from those shops. There's a difference between the donut my legit pastry chef friend made just for me and a big frozen microwave-cooked thing that a company has designed to be as unsatisfying and as cheap as possible. Both are not the healthiest option, but you can still eat either one and remain thin or fit- but only one is something most people are able to overeat on (because it doesn't satisfy), and only one of them is really low quality and has who knows what inside of it. Likewise, there's a world of differences between what's shown in that image and real Greek street food.

Honestly, souvlaki supposed to be a full meal, not a treat, not a side, not a snack. It's not a particularly high-cal meal, especially not compared to burgers, which can run you 600+ per shitty little burger that isn't even really filling. The way I get my pitas, it's only about 600-700 calories at most for both (if you wanna know exactly what I put in them: skewers, one with pork, the other one with chicken, double lettuce, and some tzatziki. I also get whole-wheat pita but they're the same cals, I just have a weird thing with white flour and products made with it), and I usually have one and half (and leave the other half for next day's lunch). Now, if you really want some filling, nutritious, but low-cal Greek food... try proper greek-style lentils. They're more like a soup, not a salad. You eat it with loads of vinegar and add a tiny bit of feta (or another dense white cheese). It's actually my fave thing on the planet.
